name: Someswara Swamy Temple, Bhimavaram
deity: Shiva worshipped as Someswara, with his consort Sri Raja Rajeswari; the complex also holds a shrine to Janardana Swamy (Vishnu)
period: Eastern Chalukya (Chalukya Bhima I), late 9th–early 10th century CE
summary: One of the five Pancharama Kshetras, this Someswara shrine in the Gunupudi quarter of Bhimavaram is famed for a linga that pales white at full moon and darkens toward the new — the Moon god's own worship set in stone.

sections.history: Someswara Swamy at Bhimavaram is counted among the five Pancharama Kshetras, the ancient Shiva temples raised where the shattered linga of Tarakasura fell across coastal Andhra. Tradition and the architecture alike point to the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, and to Chalukya Bhima I, who ruled at the turn of the tenth century; the temple in its present form is dated to the late ninth or early tenth century CE. As with its sister shrines, later centuries under the Kakatiyas, the Reddi kings and Vijayanagara added, endowed and repaired, so that the building carries the layered handiwork of several ages. Through all of it the sanctuary has remained a living place of worship, and the town of Bhimavaram — today a busy centre of West Godavari district — has grown up around a temple whose story reaches back more than a thousand years.
sections.architecture: The temple is built on two storeys, and its most extraordinary feature rises from that plan: the shrine of the goddess Annapurna sits directly above the garbhagriha, over the linga itself — an arrangement said to be found nowhere else in India, and read by devotees as Shiva bearing Ganga upon his head. A tall entrance gopuram opens the way in; before the sanctum stands a stone dhwaja-stambha some fifteen feet high, and a large Nandi keeps his watch toward the god. The presiding linga is smaller than the other four of the Pancharama circuit, pale and slender — and famous above all for its colour, which shifts with the lunar month, whitening at Pournami and deepening toward Amavasya. The temple tank, the Chandra Pushkarini or Soma Gundam, completes the lunar theme that runs through the whole kshetra.
sections.legends: The temple's names — Somarama, Someswara — carry its founding story. Here, tradition holds, the linga was installed and worshipped by Chandra, the Moon god himself, and it is to that worship that devotees trace the stone's strange lunar behaviour: white and luminous at the full moon, darkening as the moon wanes toward Amavasya, as though the linga still keeps time with the god who once tended it. The deeper origin is the shared Pancharama legend — the asura Tarakasura, made invincible by a Shiva linga he wore, could not be killed by Kartikeya until Vishnu revealed the secret; the boy-god shattered the linga with the fiery Agneyastra, and its five reuniting fragments were fixed where they fell, this one at Bhimavaram among them.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the temple's principal festival, when the night-long vigil and abhishekam draw the largest crowds of the year and the shrine keeps watch until dawn. Sri Rama Navami is celebrated with devotion, and the nine nights of Navaratri honour the goddess Sri Raja Rajeswari with special worship and adornment. On these days the timings extend well beyond the ordinary, and the Gunupudi streets around the temple fill with pilgrims.
sections.experience: To come to Somarama is to feel the moon woven through a Shiva temple. Pass beneath the great gopuram, by the fifteen-foot stone pillar and the patient Nandi, and enter the two-storeyed sanctum where the small pale linga waits — and then remember to look up, for above the garbhagriha the goddess Annapurna is enshrined as she is nowhere else in India. Devotees time their visit to the moon, hoping to see the linga white at Pournami; many pause too at the Chandra Pushkarini tank and at the Janardana Swamy shrine before they leave.

visit.timings: Open daily, roughly 6 am to 12 noon and again from 4 pm to 8 pm; timings extend on Maha Shivaratri, Sri Rama Navami and during Navaratri.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected; footwear is left outside before entering the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer areas of the temple but not within the inner sanctum.
visit.gettingThere: Bhimavaram is served by two railway stations, Bhimavaram Town and Bhimavaram Junction; the nearest airports are Rajahmundry (RJA) and Vijayawada (VGA), both well connected by road, and the temple lies in the Gunupudi area of the town.
